films.name: HP5 Plus

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, core–shell crystals of moderate size. Grain is visible at 35 mm but groups rather than speckles, and it is the grain that carries the tonality.

reciprocity.value: No correction to 1 s; +½ stop at 2 s, +1 at 10 s, +2 at 100 s

films.history: Ilford introduced HP5 in 1976 as its fast general-purpose film, and revised it as HP5 Plus in 1989 — a finer, more controllable emulsion that kept the speed. It became the reference documentary and photojournalism film in Britain, and after Ilford's 2005 receivership and the management buyout that followed, it stayed in production without a break. It is still made in Mobberley, and it is the film most people mean when they say the word 'Ilford'.

characteristics.label: Sharpness
characteristics.value: Good rather than maximal: the grain is the point, and the acutance suits enlargement at moderate size.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: One of the best pushable films made. EI 800–1600 is routine, EI 3200 gives a hard, grainy look that many photographers choose deliberately.

characteristics.label: Base
characteristics.value: Grey-blue tinted triacetate (135) or polyester (sheet). The anti-halation layer is behind the emulsion.

characteristics.label: Wet strength
characteristics.value: Robust. It survives a hot wash and rough handling better than most tabular films.

films.notes: The workhorse. Holds shadow detail well when rated at its box speed and forgiving of a stop either way.

films.name: FP4 Plus

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, finer and more even than HP5. In a fine-grain developer it prints nearly grainless at 120.

reciprocity.value: No correction to 1 s; +½ stop at 2 s, +1 at 10 s

films.history: FP4 was Ilford's fine-grain 125 film from 1968 — the 'FP' stands for Fine grain Panchromatic — and FP4 Plus replaced it in 1990 with a sharper, more modern emulsion. It has always been the quiet, unfashionable member of the Ilford range, and it is the film many landscape and architectural photographers settle on after trying everything else.

characteristics.label: Sharpness
characteristics.value: Very high. Its acutance is one reason it holds detail with fewer pixels of grain than faster stocks.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Poor beyond +1 stop. Rate it at EI 200 at most; beyond that the shadows go dead.

characteristics.label: Base
characteristics.value: Grey-blue tinted triacetate, or polyester sheet.

films.name: Delta

grainStructure.value: Flat, tabular core–shell crystals (Ilford calls the family 'Core-Shell Crystal' technology). Plate-like grains lie parallel to the base, which gives fine grain and a long straight line.

reciprocity.value: No correction to 1 s; +½ stop at 2 s, +1½ at 10 s, +2½ at 100 s

films.history: Delta 100 arrived in 1992 as Ilford's first tabular-grain film and the first serious answer to Kodak's T-Max. It has been through one quiet revision since and remains the sharpest emulsion in the Ilford range. Its long straight line makes it a favourite for copying and for work that will be digitally inverted.

characteristics.label: Sharpness
characteristics.value: Exceptional. At 120 it resolves as much as most lenses can deliver.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Holds +1 stop well; +2 works in Microphen but contrast climbs fast.

characteristics.label: Developer choice
characteristics.value: Sensitive to developer: fine-grain developers give a glassy look, Rodinal at 1+50 gives edge sharpness with visible grain and a compensating effect.

films.name: Delta

grainStructure.value: Tabular core–shell crystals: a fast film with the grain profile of a slower conventional one. The plate-like grains give smooth midtones with little clumping.

reciprocity.value: No correction to 1 s; +½ stop at 2 s, +1 at 10 s, +2 at 100 s

films.history: Delta 400 launched in 1990, the second of the Delta tabular films, and was revised in 2004 to reduce grain further. It sits between HP5's classic grain and T-Max 400's smoothness, and it is Ilford's recommendation for anyone who wants 400 speed without the grain of a conventional emulsion.

characteristics.label: Sharpness
characteristics.value: High, though softer in the shadows than Delta 100 until developed in a fine-grain developer.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Confident to EI 800; EI 1600 is usable with a contrast penalty.

films.name: Delta

grainStructure.value: Tabular crystals grown large on purpose. The grain is the image: at 3200 it looks like poured sand, and in fine-grain developers it softens into something closer to a pushed 400.

films.history: Delta 3200 was introduced in 1998 as Ilford's ultra-fast film, and it is the only 3200-speed black-and-white emulsion still in production. Its nominal ISO is a marketing figure: the emulsion's real speed is around EI 1000–1250, and the box speed is achieved by developing to a higher contrast index. That is why every published time for it is a compromise, and why two photographers' 'Delta 3200 at 3200' rarely look alike.

characteristics.label: True speed
characteristics.value: About EI 1000–1250 in a normal developer. Box speed means 'develop for 3200', not 'the film is 3200'.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Rated at 1600 in DD-X it is superb; at 3200 it is dramatic; at 6400 it is a special effect.

characteristics.label: Latent image
characteristics.value: Short. Develop within a few weeks of exposure, and keep the exposed film cool.

films.notes: Its published ISO is a nominal figure; most workers rate it at 1600 and develop to suit.

films.name: Pan F Plus

grainStructure.value: Very fine conventional cubic grain. At 120 it is effectively grainless, and that is the reason to shoot it.

films.history: Pan F dates from the late 1950s and Pan F Plus is the 1990s revision of the same idea: the slowest, finest-grain film Ilford makes. It is a film with a temperament — its latent image fades quickly, so an exposed roll left in a drawer for months loses shadow detail, and its contrast builds fast in development.

characteristics.label: Latent image
characteristics.value: Short keeping. Develop within weeks; the shadows go first.

characteristics.label: Contrast
characteristics.value: Builds quickly. Pull development by 10–20% if the scene is already contrasty.

characteristics.label: Use
characteristics.value: Best for bright light, still subjects and tripod work — the opposite of a street film.

films.notes: Latent image keeping is short — develop soon after exposure.

films.name: SFX

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, similar in size to HP5's, with the extra red sensitivity carried by a sensitising dye rather than by a different crystal.

films.history: SFX 200 appeared in the late 1990s as a black-and-white film with extended red sensitivity, reaching to about 740 nm. With a deep red filter the sky turns almost black and skin goes smooth; without one it behaves like a slightly odd 200-speed film. It is the nearest thing to infrared that still handles like an ordinary B&W stock.

characteristics.label: Red sensitivity
characteristics.value: Extended to roughly 740 nm. A red 25 filter is the usual starting point; an R72 needs +3 to +4 stops.

characteristics.label: Focus
characteristics.value: Focus is effectively unchanged — unlike true infrared film, SFX does not need a focus correction.

films.notes: Extended red sensitivity. Use a deep red filter for infrared-like skies.

films.name: XP2 Super

grainStructure.value: Chromogenic: the image is made of dye clouds formed around silver grains, and the silver is bleached away in the C-41 process. The visible grain is therefore soft-edged and low in contrast — the reason XP2 scans so cleanly.

films.history: XP1 was Ilford's first chromogenic monochrome film in the early 1980s; XP2 replaced it in the 1990s and XP2 Super in the early 2000s. Because it is developed in C-41, it can go through the same minilab as colour negative — historically the reason newspapers and labs liked it. It also scans with less grain than any silver film of the same speed.

characteristics.label: Development
characteristics.value: C-41 only. There are no useful black-and-white developer times for it.

characteristics.label: Exposure
characteristics.value: Rated anywhere from EI 50 to EI 800 in C-41 with no time change, because the process is fixed. Ilford suggests overexposing by about a stop for cleanest results.

characteristics.label: Printing
characteristics.value: The orange base makes optical printing awkward; it is designed for scanning and for RA-4 with a colour head.

films.notes: A black-and-white film on a colour-negative base: it is developed in C-41.

films.name: Tri-X

grainStructure.value: Classic cubic grain in a double-coated emulsion — a fast layer over a slower one, which is what gives Tri-X its long, film-like shoulder and its characteristic halation around highlights.

reciprocity.value: 1/1000 s or faster: +½ stop; 1 s: +1; 10 s: +2; 100 s: +3 (with a 10% development reduction at long times)

films.history: Tri-X is the most photographed black-and-white film ever made. Kodak introduced it for sheet film in the 1940s and as 35 mm Tri-X 400 in 1954; the 400-speed version became the standard press film of the 1960s and 1970s. The 2007 revision (TX) tightened the grain and changed the curve slightly while keeping the name and the look. Its ability to be pushed two or three stops and still print made it the film of photojournalism, and its halation — light bleeding around highlights through the film base — is a signature people now pay for.

characteristics.label: Halation
characteristics.value: Pronounced. Bright highlights bloom into the shadows, especially on 135. Many photographers expose for it deliberately; others use a pre-flash to control it.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: The classic push film. EI 1600 in Diafine or Microphen is a standard look; EI 3200 is a deliberate aesthetic.

characteristics.label: Tone
characteristics.value: Warm-shadowed, with strong separation in the midtones. The curve is straighter than modern tabular films.

characteristics.label: Emulsion generations
characteristics.value: The 1954 film, the 2007 TX revision and the 400TX of the 1990s all develop differently. Times published for one do not transfer to another.

films.name: T-Max

grainStructure.value: Kodak T-grain: flat, tabular silver halide crystals with a high surface-to-volume ratio. They lie parallel to the base, giving very fine grain, high sharpness and a long straight-line section.

reciprocity.value: 1 s: +½ stop; 10 s: +1½; 100 s: +3, with development reduced progressively

films.history: T-Max 100 was the first T-grain film, introduced in 1986, and it reset what a 100-speed film could resolve. Its reciprocity behaviour is unusually good because Kodak engineered deliberate low-intensity reciprocity failure into the crystals. It is the standard for copy work, forensic and scientific photography, and for anyone who wants a 100 film that behaves like a modern optical material rather than a classic one.

characteristics.label: Sharpness
characteristics.value: Very high — the sharpest of the T-Max films in absolute terms.

characteristics.label: Reciprocity
characteristics.value: The best of any B&W film: usable at 100 s with corrections published in the datasheet.

characteristics.label: Shadow detail
characteristics.value: Needs accurate exposure and generous development. It punishes underexposure more than Tri-X.

films.name: T-Max

grainStructure.value: Tabular T-grain crystals, double-coated. The 2007 TMY-2 revision reduced grain by about a stop's worth compared with the 1986 original while keeping the curve.

films.history: T-Max 400 arrived with T-Max 100 in 1986 and was reformulated in 2007 as TMY-2 — a genuinely different emulsion that many regard as the best 400-speed black-and-white film available. It is smoother than Tri-X, with a straighter curve and much finer grain, and it pushes almost as well. The two films are not interchangeable: T-Max 400 aims for fidelity, Tri-X for character.

characteristics.label: Grain
characteristics.value: About a stop finer than Tri-X 400, and more even across the frame.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Excellent to EI 1600 in T-Max Developer or DD-X, with a lower contrast gain than Tri-X.

characteristics.label: Generations
characteristics.value: TMY (1986) and TMY-2 (2007) are different emulsions with different times.

films.notes: The 2007 emulsion (TMY-2) is a different generation from the 1986 original. Times published for the older film do not transfer.

films.name: Plus-X

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain; the same double-coat philosophy as Tri-X, at a slower speed, which gives it a long smooth scale.

films.history: Plus-X Pan was Kodak's medium-speed professional film from the 1950s, and generations of press photographers used it alongside Tri-X for the finer reportage work. Kodak discontinued it in 2011, leaving T-Max 100 and Ilford FP4 as the surviving medium-speed options. Sealed stock still turns up and is usually still good; unsealed rolls more than a decade past date lose speed and gain fog.

characteristics.label: Tone
characteristics.value: Classic Kodak: warm shadows, gentle midtone separation, a long shoulder that holds highlights.

characteristics.label: Discontinued
characteristics.value: 2011. Expired stock develops close to its published times up to about ten years past date, then needs more time and a restrainer.

films.notes: Discontinued. Times below come from community charts for the last emulsion.

films.name: Portra

grainStructure.value: Dye clouds formed around tabular silver crystals, with the silver removed in the bleach. The grain is soft and low-contrast, which is why Portra scans and enlarges so cleanly.

films.history: Portra began in 1998 as a family of portrait films split into NC (natural colour) and VC (vivid colour), then converged into single Portra 160, 400 and 800 emulsions in 2010–2011. The 2010 reformulation made Portra 400 arguably the most latitude-tolerant colour negative ever made: it holds highlights several stops over and shadows well under, which is why wedding and editorial photographers moved to it wholesale. Its palette is deliberately restrained — pale skin, soft greens, gentle skies — and that is either the point or a limitation, depending on what is being photographed.

characteristics.label: Latitude
characteristics.value: Exceptional for a colour film. Two stops over is normal; four stops over still prints.

characteristics.label: Palette
characteristics.value: Neutral-to-warm skin, muted greens, clean neutrals. It does not saturate on its own.

characteristics.label: Push
characteristics.value: Pushes to 800 and 1600 with a modest contrast and grain increase; this is common practice for editorial work.

characteristics.label: Scanning
characteristics.value: Designed for scanning: its low contrast means a flat scan carries all the information.

films.name: Gold

grainStructure.value: Dye-cloud grain over a conventional cubic host. Coarser than Portra at the same speed, and more visible in flat areas of sky.

films.history: Kodacolor Gold arrived in 1988 as the consumer colour negative, and the Gold name survived every subsequent reformulation: Gold v6 in 1997, the current v7 from 2007, a move to Estar base in 2023, and since 2025 a directly sold Eastman Kodak line running alongside Kodak Alaris. The 120 format came back in March 2022 after decades away. Gold 200 is the current consumer film, warm and forgiving, designed to be printed by a minilab at 4×6 and to make skin look healthy. It is not a 'professional' emulsion and does not pretend to be; it is the film that most family albums were made on.

characteristics.label: Palette
characteristics.value: Warm, with strong reds and yellows. The look people mean by 'film colour'.

characteristics.label: Latitude
characteristics.value: Very wide — three stops over is usable, one under is fine.

characteristics.label: Where it shines
characteristics.value: Sunlight, and anything where warmth is an advantage.

films.name: Ektar

grainStructure.value: Dye clouds over T-grain crystals, the finest-grained colour negative Kodak makes. At 120 it is effectively grainless.

films.history: Ektar is an old Kodak name — the first Ektar films date from 1989 — revived in 2008 as a fine-grain, high-saturation colour negative aimed at landscape and commercial work. It behaves more like a slide film than a negative: narrow latitude, strong colour, deep shadows. That makes it magnificent in flat light and unforgiving in hard sun.

characteristics.label: Palette
characteristics.value: Highly saturated blues and reds, cooler than Portra. Skies go deep and strong.

characteristics.label: Latitude
characteristics.value: Narrow by negative standards. Expose for the highlights and hold the shadows.

characteristics.label: Skin
characteristics.value: Reds can go vivid. It is not a portrait film by design.

films.name: Velvia

grainStructure.value: Fujifilm's Super Fine-σ tabular grain: dye clouds around flat, uniform crystals, engineered for the finest grain in the range.

films.history: Velvia 50 launched in 1990 and became the landscape film of the 1990s — hyper-saturated reds and greens, deep shadows and almost no grain. Its original formulation used a chemical that became unavailable, so Fujifilm reformulated it in 2005 and discontinued it, then brought the old emulation back in 2007 as Velvia 50. It is a slide film with a narrow exposure window, and that is the bargain: one third of a stop matters.

characteristics.label: Saturation
characteristics.value: Extreme. Its reds and greens are the reason the word 'Velvia blue' exists.

characteristics.label: Latitude
characteristics.value: About ±½ stop. Meter carefully and bracket if in doubt.

characteristics.label: Long exposure
characteristics.value: Reciprocity failure from about 1/4000 s upward; +1/3 stop at 1 s, +1 at 10 s.

films.notes: Colour transparency. E-6 process, and unforgiving of exposure error.

films.name: Acros

grainStructure.value: Super Fine-σ core–shell crystals: fine, even, and unusually resistant to grain growth on long exposures.

reciprocity.value: No correction needed to 120 s; +½ stop at 1000 s — the flattest reciprocity curve of any B&W film

films.history: Acros 100 was introduced in 1998 and discontinued in 2018 when Fujifilm cut its black-and-white line. Acros 100 II arrived in 2019 — a reformulated emulsion made at a different plant, thinner-coated and with slightly different tonality from the original. The original's extraordinary reciprocity behaviour is what people miss most: Acros could be exposed for minutes without correction, which made it the night-photography film of choice.

characteristics.label: Reciprocity
characteristics.value: Outstanding. No correction to about two minutes, and less than a stop at 1000 s.

characteristics.label: Tone
characteristics.value: Cool and neutral, with a very smooth highlight roll-off. Less 'vintage' than Tri-X.

characteristics.label: Generations
characteristics.value: Acros 100 (1998–2018) and Acros 100 II (2019–) are different emulsions. Times for one do not transfer exactly.

films.notes: The II is a different emulsion from the original Acros 100.

films.name: Vision3 250D

grainStructure.value: T-grain dye-cloud emulsion with a carbon (rem-jet) backing. The backing is there to stop light piping and static in a motion-picture camera, and it must be removed before any still process.

films.history: Vision3 replaced Vision2 in 2007 as Kodak's motion-picture colour negative family, and 250D (5207) is the daylight-balanced mid-speed stock. It is designed to be printed onto another film and projected, so it is flat and low-contrast by still-photography standards — which is exactly what makes it good for scanning and grading. The 'D' is daylight balance, and it is the stock most often cut down and sold to still photographers as respools after the rem-jet is removed.

characteristics.label: Balance
characteristics.value: Daylight (5500 K). Tungsten stock is 500T.

characteristics.label: Contrast
characteristics.value: Low, by design. It expects a print or a grade to place the contrast.

characteristics.label: Backing
characteristics.value: Rem-jet carbon backing. ECN-2's alkaline pre-bath removes it; C-41 does not.

characteristics.label: Respooled as
characteristics.value: CineStill 400D, Hitchcock 250D, Silbersalz 250D and many white-label respools.

films.notes: Cinema stock on a rem-jet base. Needs an ECN-2 pre-bath; C-41 kits will not remove the backing.

films.name: Double-X 5222

grainStructure.value: Conventional cubic grain, double-coated — the same idea as Tri-X, in motion-picture form.

films.history: Double-X 5222 has been in continuous production since 1959, which makes it one of the longest-lived emulsions still made. It is Kodak's black-and-white motion-picture negative, famously used on Schindler's List and Raging Bull, and it is still the stock cinematographers reach for when they want a classic black-and-white look. Cut down into cassettes it is sold by several respoolers, and it goes through ordinary B&W chemistry once the rem-jet backing is out of the way.

characteristics.label: Look
characteristics.value: The classic cinema B&W image: deep, detailed shadows and a strong shoulder.

characteristics.label: Backing
characteristics.value: Rem-jet carbon backing. Pre-soak in an alkaline bath or remove it before development; never put it in a shared fixer.

characteristics.label: Respooled as
characteristics.value: CineStill BwXX and several other 'XX' respools.

films.notes: A black-and-white cinema stock; often developed in ordinary B&W chemistry after the rem-jet is removed.

films.name: Fomapan

grainStructure.value: Classic single-run cubic grain, coarser and more irregular than modern tabular films. It prints with the rough, almost retro texture Foma is valued for.

films.history: Foma Bohemia, in Hradec Králové, has made film since 1921 and is one of the last European manufacturers still coating black-and-white stock at scale. Fomapan 400 is the fast member of the range and has a reputation for being closer to 250 in real speed, with coarse grain and a contrast that builds quickly. Its price is the reason it survives, and its look — slightly old-fashioned, with strong red sensitivity — is why people keep buying it.

characteristics.label: True speed
characteristics.value: Many workers rate it at EI 200–320. At box speed the shadows are thin.

characteristics.label: Spectral sensitivity
characteristics.value: Extended red relative to Ilford films; skin and brickwork render warmer in tone.

characteristics.label: Coating
characteristics.value: Occasionally reports of pinholing or uneven coating on 120; check backing paper before loading.

films.notes: Classic-grain emulsion. Rate closer to ISO 250 for finer results.
